plan.outcome7: By day 7 you'll be able to take a claim like 'you should always keep your promises', ask the 4 questions philosophers ask of it (what does it mean, how would we know, is it right, who gets to decide), name one thinker who tackled each question and say in a sentence what they argued.
plan.horizon14: Later, around day 14, you could read one short original text, such as Plato's Apology, and follow the argument without a guide.
plan.horizon28: Later, around day 28, you could explain how one modern debate, such as free speech or AI rights, repeats an argument from 2,000 years ago.

picture.name: A long argument
picture.line: Western philosophy is one dinner-table argument that has run for about 2,500 years, where each new guest answers the one who spoke before, so you only need to know who is replying to whom.

chapters.title: What counts as a good argument
chapters.covers: A claim, the reasons behind it, and how to spot when the reasons do not actually support the claim, using 3 everyday examples.
chapters.outcome: You can take any opinion, split it into its claim and its reasons, and say whether the reasons hold it up.
chapters.hook: Athens put a 70-year-old man to death for asking questions. What was so dangerous?

chapters.title: Socrates and the habit of asking why
chapters.covers: How Socrates questioned people in Athens around 400 BC, why it got him executed, and how to run his question-and-answer method on your own beliefs.
chapters.outcome: You can ask 5 'why' questions in a row about a belief you hold and notice where your answers run out.
chapters.hook: Plato's best student spent 20 years with him, then told him he had it backwards.

chapters.title: Plato and Aristotle: is the real world the one we see?
chapters.covers: Plato's cave story and his idea that perfect forms sit behind everyday things, then Aristotle's reply that we learn by looking closely at the world itself.
chapters.outcome: You can explain the cave story in 3 sentences and say which side, Plato or Aristotle, a scientist is closer to.
chapters.hook: For a thousand years the argument had a referee: God. Then the referee needed defending.

chapters.title: Descartes and the question of what we can know
chapters.covers: Descartes doubting everything in 1641 until he hit one thing he could not doubt, and why that moved the argument from the world to the mind.
chapters.outcome: You can explain 'I think, therefore I am' and say what problem it was trying to solve.
chapters.hook: Could you be dreaming right now? Descartes took that question seriously, and found one thing he couldn't doubt.

chapters.title: Hume and Kant: where knowledge comes from
chapters.covers: Hume's claim that everything we know comes through the senses and habit, and Kant's reply that the mind brings its own rules to experience.
chapters.outcome: You can explain, with the example of cause and effect, why Hume said we never actually see one thing cause another and how Kant answered.
chapters.hook: Hume argued you have never once seen one thing cause another. Hard to refute.

chapters.title: How should I act: Mill against Kant
chapters.covers: Two rival tests for right and wrong: Mill's 'does it produce the most happiness' and Kant's 'could everyone act this way', applied to the same 3 dilemmas.
chapters.outcome: You can run one moral dilemma through both tests and say where they give different answers.
chapters.hook: Kant said he was waking from Hume's challenge. His fix changed the argument for 200 years.

chapters.title: Nietzsche and the modern turn: who decides what is true or good
chapters.covers: Nietzsche's challenge in the 1880s that our values have a history and were made by people, and how that question still shapes today's arguments about truth and power.
chapters.outcome: You can hear a modern claim such as 'that is just your opinion' and place it in the long argument, naming which earlier thinker it echoes and who would push back.
chapters.hook: Wittgenstein said most philosophical problems are language misfiring. If he's right, what was the argument about?

hooksFrom.outcome7: By day 7 you'll be able to tell the 2,400-year story of Western philosophy as one running argument: name about 12 key thinkers in order, say in one line what question each was answering, and explain how each answer created the problem the next thinker took up.
hooksFrom.horizon14: Later, maybe by day 14: read a short primary text (a Plato dialogue, Descartes' first Meditation) and spot which move in the argument it is making.
hooksFrom.horizon28: Later still, by day 28 if you keep going: pick one live debate (free will, what makes an act right, whether truth is objective) and lay out the two strongest sides with the thinkers behind each.

picture.name: a long dinner argument
picture.line: Western philosophy is one dinner-table argument that has run for 2,400 years: each new guest sits down, hears the last claim, and says 'yes, but'.

chapters.title: The question that started the argument
chapters.covers: Socrates in Athens, around 400 BC: why he asked 'what do you actually mean?' until it got him executed, and why that one habit is the whole method.
chapters.outcome: You can explain what Socrates was doing when he questioned people, and run a three-step Socratic check on any claim.
chapters.hook: Athens put a 70-year-old man to death for asking questions. What was so dangerous?

chapters.title: Plato's perfect world and Aristotle's messy one
chapters.covers: Plato's answer to Socrates (true things live in a perfect world beyond the senses) and his student Aristotle's reply (no, look at the actual things in front of you).
chapters.outcome: You can state Plato's and Aristotle's answers to 'where does truth live?' and say which one a modern scientist sounds like.
chapters.hook: Plato's best student spent 20 years with him, then told him he had it backwards.

chapters.title: Faith takes the chair for a thousand years
chapters.covers: How Augustine fitted Plato to Christianity and Aquinas fitted Aristotle to it, and why the question shifted from 'what is true?' to 'how do reason and God fit together?'
chapters.outcome: You can explain why Augustine and Aquinas count as philosophers and not just churchmen, and what question they handed to the next guest.
chapters.hook: For a thousand years the argument had a referee: God. Then the referee needed defending.

chapters.title: Descartes doubts everything and finds one solid floor
chapters.covers: Descartes in the 1600s wiping the table clean: doubt every belief, keep the one that survives ('I think, therefore I am'), and rebuild knowledge from there.
chapters.outcome: You can walk through Descartes' doubt step by step and explain why 'I think, therefore I am' is meant to be the one unshakeable fact.
chapters.hook: Could you be dreaming right now? Descartes took that question seriously, and found one thing he couldn't doubt.

chapters.title: The great split: trust your reason or trust your senses
chapters.covers: Locke and Hume saying all knowledge comes in through the senses, Descartes' heirs saying reason gets there first, and Hume's unsettling claim that we never actually see cause and effect.
chapters.outcome: You can say what the rationalist side and the empiricist side each claim, and explain Hume's problem with cause and effect in plain words.
chapters.hook: Hume argued you have never once seen one thing cause another. Hard to refute.

chapters.title: Kant's truce and the century of big systems
chapters.covers: Kant in the 1780s combining both sides (the mind shapes what it receives), then Hegel, Marx and Nietzsche each taking Kant's move somewhere he never intended.
chapters.outcome: You can explain Kant's compromise in one sentence and trace how it leads, step by step, to Marx's view of history and Nietzsche's 'God is dead'.
chapters.hook: Kant said he was waking from Hume's challenge. His fix changed the argument for 200 years.

chapters.title: The argument today: words, choices and minds
chapters.covers: The 1900s split into two tables: analytic philosophers (Russell, Wittgenstein) asking what sentences mean, and existentialists (Sartre, de Beauvoir) asking how to live without a given purpose, plus where the live questions sit now.
chapters.outcome: You can describe the two main ways philosophy is done today, place the whole 2,400-year story on one page, and name the question you would ask next.
chapters.hook: Wittgenstein said most philosophical problems are language misfiring. If he's right, what was the argument about?
